Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride), or TURP surgery
Low-sodium diet, spironolactone + furosemide for ascites, lactulose/rifaximin for encephalopathy, and propranolol for varices
Continuous nebulized salbutamol/ipratropium, IV corticosteroids, and IV magnesium sulfate
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Febrile Neutropenia involves empiric iv anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, or meropenem) within 60 minutes.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Thermal Burns (Major >20% TBSA)?
o: NPO, nasogastric tube decompression, IV fluids with potassium correction, and surgery if strangulated
Oral KCl for mild/moderate cases or diluted IV KCl infusion (max 10 mEq/hr peripherally) for severe cases
Corticosteroids for acute induction, immunomodulators (azathioprine), and anti-TNF biologics
Parkland formula fluid resuscitation (4 mL x kg x %TBSA of Lactated Ringer's: half in first 8h from burn time, half in next 16h)
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Thermal Burns (Major >20% TBSA) involves parkland formula fluid resuscitation (4 ml x kg x %tbsa of lactated ringer's: half in first 8h from burn time, half in next 16h).

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Compartment Syndrome (Orthopedic Emergency)?
o: IV 10% calcium gluconate slowly for acute tetany followed by oral calcium and calcitriol
Early disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs — methotrexate first-line) plus short-term steroids/NSAIDs
Immediate bivalving/removal of cast and emergent surgical fasciotomy
Low-sodium diet, spironolactone + furosemide for ascites, lactulose/rifaximin for encephalopathy, and propranolol for varices
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Compartment Syndrome (Orthopedic Emergency) involves immediate bivalving/removal of cast and emergent surgical fasciotomy.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Fat Embolism Syndrome (Long-Bone Fracture)?
o: High-flow oxygen/mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic support, and early surgical fracture stabilization
Prostaglandin analog eye drops (latanoprost) or beta-blocker drops (timolol) lifelong
Early disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs — methotrexate first-line) plus short-term steroids/NSAIDs
High-dose NSAIDs (ibuprofen/aspirin) combined with colchicine
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Fat Embolism Syndrome (Long-Bone Fracture) involves high-flow oxygen/mechanical ventilation, hemodynamic support, and early surgical fracture stabilization.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Hip Fracture & Total Hip Arthroplasty?
o: Immediate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) plus IV dexamethasone
Early oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) started within 72 hours of onset plus eye lubrication
Surgical internal fixation or arthroplasty with postoperative DVT prophylaxis (LMWH/SCDs)
Aggressive 0.9% NaCl fluid resuscitation FIRST, followed by IV regular insulin infusion and potassium replacement
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Hip Fracture & Total Hip Arthroplasty involves surgical internal fixation or arthroplasty with postoperative dvt prophylaxis (lmwh/scds).

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Osteomyelitis?
o: Strict fluid restriction (800–1000 mL/day), 3% hypertonic saline for severe neurological symptoms, or tolvaptan
Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride), or TURP surgery
High-dose NSAIDs (ibuprofen/aspirin) combined with colchicine
4–6 weeks of culture-specific IV antibiotics and surgical debridement of necrotic bone (sequestrum)
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Osteomyelitis involves 4–6 weeks of culture-specific iv antibiotics and surgical debridement of necrotic bone (sequestrum).

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Rheumatoid Arthritis?
o: Immediate IM epinephrine (1:1000, 0.3–0.5 mg) into anterolateral mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
Early disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs — methotrexate first-line) plus short-term steroids/NSAIDs
Lung-protective low-tidal-volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW), optimal PEEP, and prone positioning
Empirical antibiotics (beta-lactam + macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone) guided by CURB-65
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Rheumatoid Arthritis involves early disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (dmards — methotrexate first-line) plus short-term steroids/nsaids.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)?
o: Hydroxychloroquine for all patients, corticosteroids for flares, and immunosuppressants (mycophenolate) for nephritis
Early oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) started within 72 hours of onset plus eye lubrication
Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride), or TURP surgery
Complete, permanent cessation of all tobacco products plus vasodilators (iloprost/calcium channel blockers)
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) involves hydroxychloroquine for all patients, corticosteroids for flares, and immunosuppressants (mycophenolate) for nephritis.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Gout (Acute Gouty Arthritis)?
o: IV beta-blockers (esmolol/labetalol) first to lower HR <60 and SBP 100–120 mmHg, plus emergent surgery for Type A
NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or corticosteroids for acute flare; allopurinol for chronic prevention
Surgical internal fixation or arthroplasty with postoperative DVT prophylaxis (LMWH/SCDs)
Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride), or TURP surgery
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Gout (Acute Gouty Arthritis) involves nsaids (indomethacin), colchicine, or corticosteroids for acute flare; allopurinol for chronic prevention.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Anaphylactic Shock?
o: Aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase), and telemetry monitoring
Immediate IM epinephrine (1:1000, 0.3–0.5 mg) into anterolateral mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
Corticosteroids (prednisolone), ACE inhibitors to reduce proteinuria, and loop diuretics for edema
Immediate bivalving/removal of cast and emergent surgical fasciotomy
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Anaphylactic Shock involves immediate im epinephrine (1:1000, 0.3–0.5 mg) into anterolateral mid-thigh (vastus lateralis).

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Septic Shock?
o: Surviving Sepsis 1-hour bundle: cultures, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloids, and norepinephrine first-line vasopressor
Lifelong intramuscular cyanocobalamin/hydroxocobalamin injections (especially in pernicious anemia)
IV levothyroxine (T4) plus IV hydrocortisone (to cover possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency)
Short-acting bronchodilators (salbutamol + ipratropium), systemic corticosteroids, and controlled O2 (88–92%)
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Septic Shock involves surviving sepsis 1-hour bundle: cultures, iv broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 ml/kg crystalloids, and norepinephrine first-line vasopressor.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma?
o: Proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole) plus clarithromycin/amoxicillin or bismuth quadruple therapy for H. pylori
Prostaglandin analog eye drops (latanoprost) or beta-blocker drops (timolol) lifelong
Lung-protective low-tidal-volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW), optimal PEEP, and prone positioning
Low-sodium diet, spironolactone + furosemide for ascites, lactulose/rifaximin for encephalopathy, and propranolol for varices
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma involves prostaglandin analog eye drops (latanoprost) or beta-blocker drops (timolol) lifelong.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma?
o: Low-sodium diet (<1.5–2 g/day), thiazide diuretics, betahistine, and meclizine during acute attacks
Graduated compression stockings, leg elevation, and endovenous laser ablation or sclerotherapy
IV acetazolamide, IV mannitol, topical pilocarpine (miotic), and definitive laser peripheral iridotomy
Carbidopa-levodopa (gold standard) and dopamine agonists (pramipexole/ropinirole)
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma involves iv acetazolamide, iv mannitol, topical pilocarpine (miotic), and definitive laser peripheral iridotomy.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Retinal Detachment?
o: Pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckling, or pars plana vitrectomy
Restore renal perfusion with isotonic fluids in prerenal AKI, stop nephrotoxins, and dialyze for AEIOU indications
Continuous nebulized salbutamol/ipratropium, IV corticosteroids, and IV magnesium sulfate
IV alteplase (tPA) within 4.5 hours of last known well (if eligible) or mechanical thrombectomy
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Retinal Detachment involves pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckling, or pars plana vitrectomy.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Meniere Disease?
o: Low-sodium diet (<1.5–2 g/day), thiazide diuretics, betahistine, and meclizine during acute attacks
Therapeutic thoracentesis (removing <=1000–1500 mL at once) and treating underlying cause
Immediate therapeutic anticoagulation (heparin/LMWH) or systemic thrombolysis if hemodynamically unstable
IV acetazolamide, IV mannitol, topical pilocarpine (miotic), and definitive laser peripheral iridotomy
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Meniere Disease involves low-sodium diet (<1.5–2 g/day), thiazide diuretics, betahistine, and meclizine during acute attacks.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Cataract & Post-Cataract Surgery?
o: Treat underlying trigger (sepsis/abruptio) aggressively plus platelets, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate
Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation
Corticosteroids (prednisolone), ACE inhibitors to reduce proteinuria, and loop diuretics for edema
Sodium/fluid restriction, antihypertensives, loop diuretics, and antibiotics if active infection remains
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Cataract & Post-Cataract Surgery involves phacoemulsification with intraocular lens (iol) implantation.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with HIV / AIDS & Opportunistic Infections?
o: Therapeutic thoracentesis (removing <=1000–1500 mL at once) and treating underlying cause
IV levothyroxine (T4) plus IV hydrocortisone (to cover possible coexisting adrenal insufficiency)
Immediate needle decompression followed by tube thoracostomy connected to water-seal drainage
Lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy (ART — e.g., TDF + 3TC + Dolutegravir) plus cotrimoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 <200
e: Evidence-based first-line management of HIV / AIDS & Opportunistic Infections involves lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy (art — e.g., tdf + 3tc + dolutegravir) plus cotrimoxazole prophylaxis when cd4 <200.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever?
o: IV osmotic diuretics (mannitol 20% or 3% hypertonic saline) and CSF drainage
Careful isotonic crystalloid fluid management and acetaminophen ONLY for fever
NPO bowel rest, aggressive IV crystalloid hydration, and IV opioid analgesia
Desmopressin (DDAVP) intranasal/oral/IV and hypotonic fluid replacement
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever involves careful isotonic crystalloid fluid management and acetaminophen only for fever.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Tetanus (Clostridium tetani)?
o: IV loop diuretics (furosemide), ACE inhibitors/ARNI, and beta-blockers once stabilized
IV osmotic diuretics (mannitol 20% or 3% hypertonic saline) and CSF drainage
Human Tetanus Immunoglobulin (TIG), IV metronidazole, benzodiazepines (diazepam) for spasms, and airway protection
Surviving Sepsis 1-hour bundle: cultures, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloids, and norepinephrine first-line vasopressor
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Tetanus (Clostridium tetani) involves human tetanus immunoglobulin (tig), iv metronidazole, benzodiazepines (diazepam) for spasms, and airway protection.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Psoriasis Vulgaris?
o: Topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs (calcipotriol), phototherapy (narrowband UVB), or biologics
Titratable IV antihypertensives (nicardipine, labetalol, or clevidipine) to reduce MAP by <=25% in first hour
NPO, nasogastric tube decompression, IV fluids with potassium correction, and surgery if strangulated
Massive IV isotonic fluid replacement followed by low-dose IV regular insulin and electrolyte correction
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Psoriasis Vulgaris involves topical corticosteroids, vitamin d analogs (calcipotriol), phototherapy (narrowband uvb), or biologics.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN?
o: Strict fluid restriction (800–1000 mL/day), 3% hypertonic saline for severe neurological symptoms, or tolvaptan
Immediate discontinuation of offending drug (sulfonamides, allopurinol, carbamazepine) and burn-unit supportive care
Sit patient upright immediately, check/unkink urinary catheter or relieve fecal impaction, then give rapid vasodilator
Isotonic 0.9% NaCl for hypovolemic, fluid restriction for euvolemic (SIADH), or 3% hypertonic saline for seizures
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN involves immediate discontinuation of offending drug (sulfonamides, allopurinol, carbamazepine) and burn-unit supportive care.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Hypokalemia (Serum K+ <3.5 mEq/L)?
o: Primary PCI within 90 minutes (or fibrinolysis within 30 min) plus aspirin and dual antiplatelet therapy
IV beta-blockers (esmolol/labetalol) first to lower HR <60 and SBP 100–120 mmHg, plus emergent surgery for Type A
Complete, permanent cessation of all tobacco products plus vasodilators (iloprost/calcium channel blockers)
Oral KCl for mild/moderate cases or diluted IV KCl infusion (max 10 mEq/hr peripherally) for severe cases
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Hypokalemia (Serum K+ <3.5 mEq/L) involves oral kcl for mild/moderate cases or diluted iv kcl infusion (max 10 meq/hr peripherally) for severe cases.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Hyperkalemia (Serum K+ >5.5 mEq/L)?
o: Isotonic 0.9% NaCl for hypovolemic, fluid restriction for euvolemic (SIADH), or 3% hypertonic saline for seizures
IV 10% calcium gluconate FIRST to stabilize myocardium, then IV regular insulin + D50W, nebulized albuterol, and dialysis
NPO bowel rest, aggressive IV crystalloid hydration, and IV opioid analgesia
Immediate needle decompression followed by tube thoracostomy connected to water-seal drainage
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Hyperkalemia (Serum K+ >5.5 mEq/L) involves iv 10% calcium gluconate first to stabilize myocardium, then iv regular insulin + d50w, nebulized albuterol, and dialysis.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Hyponatremia (Serum Na+ <135 mEq/L)?
o: Treat underlying trigger (sepsis/abruptio) aggressively plus platelets, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate
Isotonic 0.9% NaCl for hypovolemic, fluid restriction for euvolemic (SIADH), or 3% hypertonic saline for seizures
Short-acting bronchodilators (salbutamol + ipratropium), systemic corticosteroids, and controlled O2 (88–92%)
Immediate discontinuation of offending drug (sulfonamides, allopurinol, carbamazepine) and burn-unit supportive care
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Hyponatremia (Serum Na+ <135 mEq/L) involves isotonic 0.9% nacl for hypovolemic, fluid restriction for euvolemic (siadh), or 3% hypertonic saline for seizures.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Hypercalcemia (Serum Ca2+ >10.5 mg/dL)?
o: Alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride), or TURP surgery
Sodium/fluid restriction, antihypertensives, loop diuretics, and antibiotics if active infection remains
Aggressive IV 0.9% NaCl hydration, IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid), and calcitonin
Continuous nebulized salbutamol/ipratropium, IV corticosteroids, and IV magnesium sulfate
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Hypercalcemia (Serum Ca2+ >10.5 mg/dL) involves aggressive iv 0.9% nacl hydration, iv bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid), and calcitonin.

q: What is the recommended first-line medical management for a patient diagnosed with Pulmonary Edema (Acute Cardiogenic)?
o: High-flow O2 / NIV (CPAP/BiPAP), IV furosemide, IV nitroglycerin, and careful morphine if indicated
4–6 weeks of culture-specific IV antibiotics and surgical debridement of necrotic bone (sequestrum)
IV 10% calcium gluconate FIRST to stabilize myocardium, then IV regular insulin + D50W, nebulized albuterol, and dialysis
Empirical antibiotics (beta-lactam + macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone) guided by CURB-65
e: Evidence-based first-line management of Pulmonary Edema (Acute Cardiogenic) involves high-flow o2 / niv (cpap/bipap), iv furosemide, iv nitroglycerin, and careful morphine if indicated.

q: When caring for a patient with Acute Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Administer oxygen if SpO2 <90%, obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, and maintain continuous telemetry
Monitor ECG for peaked T waves (hyperkalemia), record strict hourly urine output, and weigh patient daily
NEVER administer mydriatic/anticholinergic drops (atropine) which worsen angle closure; treat as ophthalmic emergency
Advise strict broad-spectrum sunscreen/sun avoidance and monitor urinalysis/creatinine routinely for lupus nephritis
e: Priority nursing management in Acute Myocardial Infarction (STEMI): Administer oxygen if SpO2 <90%, obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, and maintain continuous telemetry. Failure to act promptly risks ventricular fibrillation and cardiogenic shock.

q: When caring for a patient with Left-Sided Heart Failure, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Recognize a sudden 'silent chest' with rising PaCO2 as an airway emergency requiring immediate intubation prep
Give levodopa separately from high-protein meals, encourage wide-based gait, and implement fall precautions
Place patient in high-Fowler's position, monitor daily weights, and track strict intake/output
Keep IV calcium gluconate and emergency tracheostomy tray at bedside after thyroidectomy
e: Priority nursing management in Left-Sided Heart Failure: Place patient in high-Fowler's position, monitor daily weights, and track strict intake/output. Failure to act promptly risks acute flash pulmonary edema with pink frothy sputum.

q: When caring for a patient with Right-Sided Heart Failure (Cor Pulmonale), which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Initiate droplet isolation for first 24 hours of antibiotic therapy and dim room lights for photophobia
Monitor NG output color/volume, serial abdominal girth, and alert surgeon immediately for fever or absent bowel sounds
Restrict dietary sodium/fluids, elevate edematous extremities, and assess daily abdominal girth
Implement seizure precautions and limit serum sodium rise to <=8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours to prevent ODS
e: Priority nursing management in Right-Sided Heart Failure (Cor Pulmonale): Restrict dietary sodium/fluids, elevate edematous extremities, and assess daily abdominal girth. Failure to act promptly risks cardiac cirrhosis and refractory anasarca.

q: When caring for a patient with Infective Endocarditis, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Titrate low-flow oxygen via Venturi mask to keep SpO2 88–92% and teach pursed-lip breathing
Administer oxygen if SpO2 <90%, obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, and maintain continuous telemetry
Correct serum sodium slowly (<=8 mEq/L in 24 hours) to prevent irreversible osmotic demyelination syndrome
Draw blood cultures BEFORE initiating empirical IV antibiotics and monitor for embolic neurological deficits
e: Priority nursing management in Infective Endocarditis: Draw blood cultures BEFORE initiating empirical IV antibiotics and monitor for embolic neurological deficits. Failure to act promptly risks septic arterial embolization causing ischemic stroke or mycotic aneurysm.

q: When caring for a patient with Cardiac Tamponade, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Secure airway EARLY if hoarseness/singed nares present and titrate fluids to maintain adult urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr
Prepare pericardiocentesis tray immediately, maintain IV access, and monitor continuous ECG during needle aspiration
Manage like a major burn: sterile non-adherent dressings, IV fluids, strict infection prevention, and ophthalmology consult
Maintain hip abduction pillow after posterior approach: avoid hip flexion >90 degrees, adduction past midline, and internal rotation
e: Priority nursing management in Cardiac Tamponade: Prepare pericardiocentesis tray immediately, maintain IV access, and monitor continuous ECG during needle aspiration. Failure to act promptly risks obstructive shock and pulseless electrical activity (pea) arrest.

q: When caring for a patient with Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Maintain bed rest with affected limb elevated and NEVER massage the swollen calf
Apply compression stockings in the morning BEFORE dangling legs out of bed and avoid prolonged standing
Administer IM epinephrine FIRST, maintain patent airway, give rapid IV 0.9% NaCl, and observe for biphasic reaction
NEVER apply heat to abdomen or give laxatives/enemas (risk of rupture); sudden pain relief signals perforation
e: Priority nursing management in Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT): Maintain bed rest with affected limb elevated and NEVER massage the swollen calf. Failure to act promptly risks life-threatening pulmonary embolism.

q: When caring for a patient with Acute Pulmonary Embolism, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Enforce neutropenic precautions: strict hand hygiene, NO rectal temperatures/enemas, no fresh flowers or raw unpeeled produce
Elevate head of bed, administer high-flow oxygen, and monitor closely for right ventricular failure
Avoid rapid precipitous BP drop to prevent cerebral hypoperfusion and monitor arterial line continuously
Protect AV fistula arm: NEVER take BP, draw blood, or start IV in fistula arm; palpate thrill and auscultate bruit daily
e: Priority nursing management in Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Elevate head of bed, administer high-flow oxygen, and monitor closely for right ventricular failure. Failure to act promptly risks obstructive shock and sudden cardiopulmonary collapse.

q: When caring for a patient with Acute Pericarditis, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Position patient upright leaning forward over bedside table and monitor for muffled heart sounds
Remember IV calcium gluconate protects the heart immediately but does NOT lower serum K+ — follow with insulin/dextrose
Draw blood cultures BEFORE initiating empirical IV antibiotics and monitor for embolic neurological deficits
Turn patient to lateral recovery position, protect head, loosen tight clothing, and NEVER insert objects into mouth
e: Priority nursing management in Acute Pericarditis: Position patient upright leaning forward over bedside table and monitor for muffled heart sounds. Failure to act promptly risks constrictive pericarditis or cardiac tamponade.

q: When caring for a patient with Hypertensive Emergency, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Initiate droplet isolation for first 24 hours of antibiotic therapy and dim room lights for photophobia
Avoid rapid precipitous BP drop to prevent cerebral hypoperfusion and monitor arterial line continuously
Enforce neutropenic precautions: strict hand hygiene, NO rectal temperatures/enemas, no fresh flowers or raw unpeeled produce
Administer pyridostigmine 30–60 minutes BEFORE meals to maximize swallowing strength and keep intubation kit ready
e: Priority nursing management in Hypertensive Emergency: Avoid rapid precipitous BP drop to prevent cerebral hypoperfusion and monitor arterial line continuously. Failure to act promptly risks intracerebral hemorrhage and acute aortic dissection.

q: When caring for a patient with Acute Aortic Dissection, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Control heart rate BEFORE adding vasodilators to prevent reflex shear stress on the aortic wall
Monitor hourly urine output, neurological status, and slow osmolar correction to avoid cerebral edema
Administer oxygen if SpO2 <90%, obtain 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, and maintain continuous telemetry
Place patient in a quiet, dark, low-stimulation room to prevent reflex spasms and keep intubation/tracheostomy equipment ready
e: Priority nursing management in Acute Aortic Dissection: Control heart rate BEFORE adding vasodilators to prevent reflex shear stress on the aortic wall. Failure to act promptly risks aortic rupture, pericardial tamponade, and limb or renal ischemia.

q: When caring for a patient with Buerger Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans), which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Instruct gentle emollient application without picking scales (prevents Koebner trauma flares)
Reinforce strict smoking cessation, inspect feet daily for trauma, and avoid cold exposure
Keep bed in low position with side rails up during vertigo attacks, move slowly, and eliminate caffeine/alcohol/nicotine
Strictly AVOID aspirin and NSAIDs (worsen bleeding); monitor for warning signs (abdominal pain, rising hematocrit with falling platelets)
e: Priority nursing management in Buerger Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans): Reinforce strict smoking cessation, inspect feet daily for trauma, and avoid cold exposure. Failure to act promptly risks digital gangrene requiring amputation.

q: When caring for a patient with Varicose Veins & Chronic Venous Insufficiency, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Apply compression stockings in the morning BEFORE dangling legs out of bed and avoid prolonged standing
Reinforce strict smoking cessation, inspect feet daily for trauma, and avoid cold exposure
Strain ALL urine through gauze to capture passed stones for chemical analysis and encourage 2.5–3 L/day fluids
Balance rest with gentle ROM exercises, apply warm moist heat for morning stiffness, and monitor LFTs/CBC on methotrexate
e: Priority nursing management in Varicose Veins & Chronic Venous Insufficiency: Apply compression stockings in the morning BEFORE dangling legs out of bed and avoid prolonged standing. Failure to act promptly risks non-healing medial malleolar venous stasis ulcer.

q: When caring for a patient with COPD Exacerbation, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Control heart rate BEFORE adding vasodilators to prevent reflex shear stress on the aortic wall
Avoid rapid precipitous BP drop to prevent cerebral hypoperfusion and monitor arterial line continuously
Maintain bed rest with affected limb elevated and NEVER massage the swollen calf
Titrate low-flow oxygen via Venturi mask to keep SpO2 88–92% and teach pursed-lip breathing
e: Priority nursing management in COPD Exacerbation: Titrate low-flow oxygen via Venturi mask to keep SpO2 88–92% and teach pursed-lip breathing. Failure to act promptly risks co2 narcosis and acute hypercapnic respiratory failure.

q: When caring for a patient with Status Asthmaticus, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Perform postural drainage and chest percussion BEFORE meals to avoid vomiting and aspiration
Recognize a sudden 'silent chest' with rising PaCO2 as an airway emergency requiring immediate intubation prep
Monitor fluid/electrolyte status, provide low-residue diet during flares, and watch for sudden abdominal distension
Draw blood cultures BEFORE IV antibiotics (without delaying >45 min) and titrate norepinephrine to keep MAP >=65 mmHg
e: Priority nursing management in Status Asthmaticus: Recognize a sudden 'silent chest' with rising PaCO2 as an airway emergency requiring immediate intubation prep. Failure to act promptly risks severe hypoxemic/hypercapnic arrest and barotrauma.

q: When caring for a patient with Tension Pneumothorax, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Perform postural drainage and chest percussion BEFORE meals to avoid vomiting and aspiration
Keep water-seal chest drainage unit below chest level and NEVER clamp a bubbling chest tube
Elevate head of bed, administer high-flow oxygen, and monitor closely for right ventricular failure
Administer pyridostigmine 30–60 minutes BEFORE meals to maximize swallowing strength and keep intubation kit ready
e: Priority nursing management in Tension Pneumothorax: Keep water-seal chest drainage unit below chest level and NEVER clamp a bubbling chest tube. Failure to act promptly risks mediastinal shift obstructing venous return and obstructive shock.

q: When caring for a patient with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Place patient in a quiet, dark, low-stimulation room to prevent reflex spasms and keep intubation/tracheostomy equipment ready
Maintain prone positioning 12–16 hours/day in severe ARDS and monitor plateau pressures <30 cmH2O
Correct serum sodium slowly (<=8 mEq/L in 24 hours) to prevent irreversible osmotic demyelination syndrome
Elevate head of bed 30 degrees with neck in neutral midline alignment and avoid coughing/straining/hip flexion
e: Priority nursing management in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): Maintain prone positioning 12–16 hours/day in severe ARDS and monitor plateau pressures <30 cmH2O. Failure to act promptly risks barotrauma, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and multiorgan failure.

q: When caring for a patient with Community-Acquired Pneumonia, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Encourage incentive spirometry, deep breathing, hydration to thin secretions, and monitor SpO2
NEVER administer mydriatic/anticholinergic drops (atropine) which worsen angle closure; treat as ophthalmic emergency
Educate on low-fat diet post-discharge and monitor for clay-colored stools/jaundice suggesting choledocholithiasis
Maintain NPO until bedside dysphagia swallow screen is passed and keep BP <185/110 mmHg prior to tPA
e: Priority nursing management in Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Encourage incentive spirometry, deep breathing, hydration to thin secretions, and monitor SpO2. Failure to act promptly risks parapneumonic empyema and septic shock.

q: When caring for a patient with Pleural Effusion, which action is the nurse's HIGHEST clinical priority?
o: Educate patients NEVER to stop steroids abruptly and to double/triple oral doses during illness or stress
